transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-21 15:00 PT
Duration: ~51 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Luis (Redwood SE), Samira (Redwood SE), Priya (QR VP Eng), Tom (QR NetEng), Leah (QR Security), Alex (QR Cloud Ops)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on QuantumRidge's private onramp readiness. Main concerns: NAT gateway / egress, region gating and data residency (EU-only projects), private endpoints vs VPC peering, and SSO/KMS for keys. Discussed potential trade-offs between hosted vs dedicated vs private (they strongly lean private due to compliance).

Topics:
- VPC peering vs Transit Gateway patterns for multi-account architecture
- Private endpoints and DNS resolution across VPCs
- Egress NAT capacity and per-hour burst rates
- Region restrictions (EU data residency, APAC later)
- Audit logs, KMS integration, and SSO (SAML/Okta)
- Test pilot and bench-marking network egress 

Action items recap (at end of call) included pricing + security docs, network diagrams, and a technical deep dive scheduled with SEs.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Alright, good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood Inference, i have Luis and Samira with me from our SE team, can we go around quick?
[00:09] Priya Nair: Yeah hi, i'm Priya with QuantumRidge, vp engineering, we've got Tom on networking and Leah on security, and Alex for cloud ops, quick background we currently run most ai inference on-prem and are evaluating private deployment options with Redwood.
[00:23] Luis Ortega: Awesome. Quick clarifying question, are you primarily looking for a VPC onramp to Redwood Private where traffic never leaves AWS backbone or do you expect some on-prem hops?
[00:35] Tom Becker: Our goal is to keep traffic inside the cloud when possible, we have a hybrid estate but the first phase is pure AWS — multi-account, centralized transit gateway. We want a design that can be later extended to on-prem via Direct Connect.
[00:48] Leah Ortiz: And security wise we need EU-only models for a subset of customers, so region gating and data residency are blockers for us. Also SOC2/audit logs and the ability to use our KMS for keys.
[01:02] Maya Chen: Makes total sense. Redwood Private supports customer-managed networking and KMS integrations, we can run dedicated instances in EU regions and tie in with your KMS/HSM — we'll share the integration doc after.
[01:16] Alex Mu: One immediate question — NAT gateway egress capacity. If we run a high QPS workload, do you have per-hour bursting limits or do we size NAT behind your private endpoints?
[01:28] Samira Patel: Good question. So typically requests to Redwood Private endpoints go over a private interface — you can use private endpoints or peering. If egresses external to your VPC are needed, you control the NAT layout in your account. If you route through Redwood-managed egress there are options but we recommend customer NAT for predictable billing.
[01:49] Tom Becker: Wait, just to be clear — if we peer our VPCs to Redwood's, do we need to open up 0.0.0.0/0 egress anywhere or everything stays internal?
[02:02] Luis Ortega: If you set up VPC peering with route tables that keep traffic on the internal AWS network, there is no public internet egress for inference traffic. However, for things like image fetching or external calls from model hooks, you'll need controlled egress or proxy. Also when using Transit Gateway you can centralize egress at a single NAT/GW.
[02:23] Leah Ortiz: How about DNS? We have split-horizon DNS and we need private endpoint resolution across accounts without leaking names to public DNS.
[02:31] Samira Patel: We typically recommend using AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints) for the control plane and model endpoints, with shared Route53 private hosted zones or resolver rules for cross-account name resolution. In some accounts we've done resolver endpoints to forward to the central zone.
[02:47] Tom Becker: Are there any limits on number of interface endpoints or per-region endpoint quotas we should plan for?
[02:54] Luis Ortega: Good call — AWS has soft limits, and while Redwood doesn't impose model endpoint counts, you'll want to request quota increases ahead of time for a large footprint. We'll include recommended quota targets in the doc.
[03:10] Priya Nair: On the hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoff, cost is a factor but compliance pushes us to private. What do other customers do if they need EU-only? Do you provision dedicated capacity inside EU?
[03:22] Maya Chen: Yes, we can provision dedicated pools in the EU region. For strict data residency many customers use Redwood Private in their VPC or a dedicated region-only Redwood deployment. We'll walk you through the deployment matrix in the follow-up doc.
[03:36] Leah Ortiz: KMS — we require key escrow via our KMS. Can Redwood use customer-managed KMS and can we rotate keys independently?
[03:46] Samira Patel: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS for storage encryption and TLS certs — key rotation is supported; you'll manage policies in your KMS. We'll attach the KMS integration guide.
[03:58] Alex Mu: Network ACLs — we already have strict deny-all inbound rules. Is there a recommended list of ports and IP ranges to allow for the private onramp?
[04:09] Luis Ortega: For PrivateLink you'd allow interface endpoints on standard TLS/443 and the control plane ranges we'll provide. If you opt for peering, route table entries to Redwood subnets suffice. We have a minimal port list but we'll put that in the packet.
[04:23] Priya Nair: Latency — our application targets 30–50ms p95 for in-app generation. Can Redwood meet that from eu-west-1 with private peering?
[04:34] Maya Chen: With regional deployment in eu-west-1 and local dedicated capacity, 30–50ms p95 is achievable for short context lengths; for larger contexts it varies. We'll share latency profiles. Noted: we should run a bench with your payload to validate.
[04:51] Tom Becker: About transit vs peering — we currently have a Transit Gateway in each region and are using centralized egress. Is it better to peer Redwood VPCs to each account or use Transit Gateway attachments?
[05:02] Luis Ortega: Both patterns are used. Transit Gateway scales better for many accounts and centralizes routing and egress, but VPC peering can be simpler for a few accounts. Transit GW allows you to apply central security controls and NAT. We'll sketch both options specific to your account topology.
[05:18] Leah Ortiz: Audit logs — we need immutable logs for all inference requests for a subset of workloads. Is there a way to stream request metadata to our log storage?
[05:26] Samira Patel: Yes, Redwood Private can emit audit logs to a customer S3 or to a SIEM via Kinesis/CloudWatch forwarding. For high compliance we recommend dedicated ingestion pipelines. We'll include the event schema sample.
[05:40] Priya Nair: Are there any IP ranges we should put on allow-lists that are stable, or do they change a lot?
[05:47] Maya Chen: For PrivateLink, interface endpoints have ENIs in your account, so you control the IPs. For Redwood-hosted egress ranges we provide stable lists and an update channel but customer-managed networking is always preferred for strict allow-listing.
[06:03] Alex Mu: One edge case — we run some training jobs that call inference asynchronously and those jobs are in a separate account. Will the cross-account invocation add significant complexity?
[06:14] Luis Ortega: Not really — you can set up cross-account roles and allow the invoking account to reach the endpoint via Transit Gateway or peering. The main complexity is auth policies and ensuring your route tables allow traffic.
[06:27] Tom Becker: Any gotchas with AWS PrivateLink in terms of scaling and bursting?
[06:33] Samira Patel: PrivateLink scales well, but you should watch ENI quotas per AZ. Also, client connections are TCP so connection churn matters — use connection pooling on the client side. We'll add pooling recommendations.
[06:47] Priya Nair: Ok, so next steps from our side — we'll compile the list of VPCs, CIDRs, NAT numbers, and the accounts to onboard. From Redwood — want the SOC2 and detailed network doc.
[06:59] Maya Chen: Exactly. We'll also prepare a recommended design: option A (Transit GW central) and option B (direct peering + interface endpoints), with an estimated egress cost model and latency expectations.
[07:14] Tom Becker: Can you also include a short runbook for failover? For example, if an AZ goes down or if an egress NAT spikes — we want automatic fallback to another region or capacity tier.
[07:23] Luis Ortega: Yes, Redwood supports failover policies — we have canary + fallback to a compatible model variant and region-level fallback. For networking failover you'd implement cross-region peering or route failover; we'll document patterns.
[07:39] Leah Ortiz: Any implications for SSO? We use Okta and want SAML/SCIM provisioning and RBAC.
[07:45] Samira Patel: Redwood Console supports SAML SSO and SCIM for provisioning, RBAC with teams and roles. We'll include the SSO integration guide and minimum attribute list.
[07:58] Alex Mu: One more question — telemetry: can we get per-token cost breakdowns and tracing correlation ids so our APM can link app requests to inference calls?
[08:07] Maya Chen: Yes, Redwood Console provides token-level cost and latency breakdowns and you can pass a correlation id on requests that gets surfaced in traces. We'll add example headers.
[08:21] Priya Nair: Great. For the pilot, can we get a small dedicated pool in eu-west-1 for a 30-day eval?
[08:30] Maya Chen: We typically run a pilot with a scoped dedicated pool or a private deployment in your VPC depending on need; i'll have sales and engineering propose sizing and pricing for a 30-day pilot.
[08:40] Tom Becker: Ok thanks, that helps. A couple of times i heard "KV cache" mentioned in your docs — is that something that requires special networking?
[08:47] Samira Patel: KV cache is internal to the model runtime and doesn't need special network configuration; it's about memory persistence and sharding. No special egress required.
[08:58] Priya Nair: Anything else we should be aware of for bringing our compliance team into the review?
[09:04] Leah Ortiz: We'll want a secure architecture diagram, encryption at rest and in transit details, and evidence of SOC2 controls.
[09:12] Maya Chen: We'll share the security pack and a proposed diagram. Also happy to set up a 1:1 with our security engineering for their questions.
[09:24] Priya Nair: Great, let's schedule the technical deep dive next week if possible, and we'll get the VPC info over.
[09:30] Maya Chen: Sounds good. We'll target the week of 9/28 for the SE deep-dive.
[09:35] Alex Mu: I'll add the VPC CIDRs to the shared doc by EOD Friday.
[09:40] Maya Chen: Perfect, we'll reconvene after you drop the network details. Thanks everyone.

[End of meeting]
